prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current perception systems for autonomous agents, particularly in 3D environments, suffer from a fundamental "inclusiveness assumption": they rely on the premise that all potential categories of interest are known beforehand. Whether using closed-set supervision or modern open-vocabulary methods, the system inevitably requires a human to provide a specific vocabulary list or text prompts. This dependency severely limits scalability and safety, as it renders the model incapable of recognizing "atypical" objects or rare road users that were not anticipated by the human operator. There is currently no framework that allows a 3D perception model to autonomously determine *what* is in a scene without external textual guidance.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose to eliminate the human-in-the-loop by inverting the standard segmentation paradigm. Instead of asking the model to find specific words in a scene, we hypothesize that we can first ask the model to *describe* the scene, and then use that description to segment it.

We posit that by combining multi-modal captioning (generating text from both images and LiDAR data) with natural language processing, we can automatically generate a scene-specific "Auto-Vocabulary" at runtime. Furthermore, we believe that relying solely on image captioning is insufficient for robust 3D perception (e.g., in low light); therefore, we hypothesize that a geometry-based point cloud captioning mechanism is required to ensure object diversity and lighting invariance.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose a framework dubbed **3D-AVS** (3D Auto-Vocabulary Segmentation). The workflow mimics a "caption-then-segment" logic:

**1. Dual-Stream Vocabulary Generation**
To generate the target labels, we will employ two parallel captioning modules:
*   **Image Captioner:** We will utilize off-the-shelf Multi-Modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to generate detailed descriptions of the visual data.
*   **Point Captioner (The "SMAP" Module):** Standard point encoders only provide a single global feature vector (and thus a single global caption), which is insufficient for dense scene understanding. We propose a **Sparse Masked Attention Pooling (SMAP)** mechanism.
    *   *Intuition:* We will geometrically partition the point cloud (e.g., into sectors or pillars) and apply binary masks to the features.
    *   *Pooling:* Instead of averaging the whole scene, we will pool features within these masked sub-regions.
    *   *Decoding:* These region-specific features will be decoded into text, ensuring we capture distinct objects rather than just a general scene summary. This allows us to generate text solely from geometry, providing robustness when cameras fail (e.g., night driving).

**2. Caption-to-Tag Parsing**
The output of the captioners will be natural language sentences. We will implement a text parsing module using NLP techniques (lemmatization and noun extraction) to distill these sentences into a concise list of unique semantic tags (nouns). This list becomes our dynamic, scene-specific vocabulary.

**3. Feature Alignment and Segmentation**
We will align the generated vocabulary and the input point cloud in a shared latent space (similar to CLIP space).
*   **Text Encoding:** The generated tags are encoded into text embeddings.
*   **Point Encoding:** The input points are encoded into visual/geometric embeddings.
*   **Assignment:** Semantic labels will be assigned to points by calculating the similarity between point features and the auto-generated text embeddings.

**4. Semantic Evaluation Strategy (TPSS)**
Standard evaluation metrics fail here because the generated vocabulary is unknown and may contain synonyms (e.g., "trash can" vs. "garbage bin"). We propose a **Text-Point Semantic Similarity (TPSS)** metric. Instead of matching string labels, we will evaluate the cosine similarity between the *embedding* of the predicted label and the *embedding* of the point in the latent space. This allows us to grade the semantic accuracy of the prediction without requiring exact string matching against a fixed dataset.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Paradigm Shift:** We aim to establish the first framework for 3D Auto-Vocabulary Segmentation, moving perception from "prompt-dependent" to "data-driven" label generation.
*   **Robustness via Geometry:** By introducing a specialized Point Captioner with Sparse Masked Attention Pooling, we expect to achieve robust semantic recognition in adverse lighting conditions where image-based methods typically fail.
*   **Evaluation Methodology:** The proposed annotation-free similarity metric (TPSS) will provide a theoretical foundation for evaluating open-ended recognition tasks where exact label matching is impossible due to synonyms and hierarchy.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We established a comprehensive framework to evaluate the proposed 3D Auto-Vocabulary Segmentation (3D-AVS) method against existing state-of-the-art methods and baselines. The setup focused on validating the method's ability to segment 3D point clouds without pre-defined vocabularies.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **nuScenes:** A real-world dataset for autonomous driving capturing urban scenarios (Boston and Singapore). We aggregated LiDAR points over a 0.5-second interval to increase spatial density. We utilized the validation set for evaluation. The official benchmark contains 16 manually annotated categories.
    *   **ScanNet:** An indoor dataset containing 3D reconstructions of indoor scenes with 20 annotated classes.
    *   **ScanNet200:** Utilizes the same point clouds as ScanNet but updates annotations to 200 finer-grained categories.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Text-Point Semantic Similarity (TPSS):** An annotation-free metric introduced to assess semantic consistency between points and text labels in CLIP space. This metric is independent of dataset annotations and subjective assessment.
    *   **mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU):** Standard segmentation metric. To calculate this for auto-generated vocabularies, we mapped the open-ended categories to the fixed ground-truth categories using an LLM-based mapper (specifically GPT-4o, which we found superior to LAVE and SBERT).

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Fixed/Official Vocabulary Methods:** CLIP2Scene, HICL, CNS, ConceptFusion, OpenMask3D, AdaCo.
    *   **Open-Vocabulary Methods:** OpenScene (tested with both Official and Extended label sets), Diff2Scene.
    *   **Variants:** 3D-AVS-Image (Image captioning only), 3D-AVS-LiDAR (Point captioning only), 3D-AVS (Combined).

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Image Captioner:** We utilized xGen-MM due to its architectural flexibility and semantic coverage. We employed beam search for caption generation.
    *   **Point Captioner:** We developed a custom Point Captioner trained via transfer learning (2D-to-3D distillation from CLIP). It utilizes a Sparse Masked Attention Pooling (SMAP) module.
    *   **Mask Generation:** For the Point Captioner, we used geometry-based mask generation (cylindrical sector-based for outdoor, square pillar-based for indoor) to partition point clouds without camera intrinsics.
    *   **Text Parsing:** We used spaCy for noun filtering and lemmatization, verified against the WordNet dictionary.
    *   **Segmenter:** We employed a pipeline separating vocabulary generation and segmentation, utilizing a text encoder, high-resolution image encoder, and point encoder aligned in CLIP latent space.
    *   **Mapping for Evaluation:** GPT-4o was used to map generated labels to fixed vocabulary classes for mIoU comparison.

## 2. Raw Numeric Data

**Table 1: Text-Point Semantic Similarity (TPSS) Score Comparison**
*This table compares the semantic consistency of labels generated by our method versus human-defined label sets on nuScenes and ScanNet validation sets.*

| Label Set Source | Human-involved in Label Set? | nuScenes TPSS Score | ScanNet TPSS Score |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Official label set | Yes | 7.39 | 3.44 |
| Extended label set | Yes | 8.70 | - |
| **3D-AVS-Image** | No | 8.78 | 3.49 |
| **3D-AVS-LiDAR** | No | 8.80 | 3.71 |
| **3D-AVS (Combined)** | No | **9.65** | **3.78** |

**Table 2: Segmentation Performance (mIoU) Comparison**
*Comparison of Intersection-over-Union on nuScenes (NUS), ScanNet (SN), and ScanNet200 (SN200). "Unknown Vocabulary" indicates if the method operates without a pre-defined list. "Official" refers to the standard dataset vocabulary.*

| Method | Unknown Vocabulary Support | Label Set Used | nuScenes (mIoU) | ScanNet (mIoU) | ScanNet200 (mIoU) |
| :--- | :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| CLIP2Scene | No | Official | 20.8 | 25.1 | - |
| ConceptFusion | No | Official | - | 33.3 | 8.8 |
| OpenMask3D | No | Official | - | 34.0 | 10.3 |
| HICL | No | Official | 26.8 | 33.5 | - |
| AdaCo | No | Official | 31.2 | - | - |
| CNS | No | Official | 33.5 | 26.8 | - |
| OpenScene | No | Official | 30.1 | 47.0 | 11.7 |
| Diff2Scene | No | Official | - | **48.6** | 14.2 |
| **3D-AVS (Ours)** | **Yes** | **I+L (Generated)** | **36.2** | 40.5 | **14.6** |

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Vocabulary Generation Analysis:**
*   **Vocabulary Size Expansion:** On the nuScenes validation set, our method recognized **671 unique categories**, significantly surpassing the original dataset's 16 categories.
*   **Semantic Precision:** We observed that while pre-defined vocabularies use ambiguous terms like "manmade," our method successfully identified specific entities such as "building" and "signboard."
*   **Specific Class Improvements:** In nuScenes, we achieved substantial mIoU improvements on ambiguous categories compared to OpenScene:
    *   "Drivable surface": 68.2 mIoU
    *   "Terrain": 41.4 mIoU
    *   "Manmade": 55.4 mIoU

**Robustness to Lighting Conditions:**
*   **Night and Rain:** We analyzed TPSS scores across different nuScenes subsets (Daylight, Night, Not-Rainy, Rainy).
*   **Modality Performance:** The LiDAR-only variant of our method outperformed the Image-only variant during "Night" and "Rainy" scenes.
*   **Synergy:** The combined approach (Image + LiDAR) consistently achieved the highest semantic similarity scores across all conditions, demonstrating that the point captioner effectively compensates when visual data is unreliable (e.g., low light).

**Visual Segmentation Analysis:**
*   **Comparison with OpenScene:** When comparing visual segmentation results, OpenScene (using pre-defined vocabulary) often produced large-area errors, misclassifying regions due to ambiguous class definitions.
*   **Fine-Grained Detection:** Our method successfully segmented and named precise objects that were otherwise grouped into coarse ground-truth categories. For example:
    *   Points annotated as "vegetation" were identified as "plant."
    *   Points annotated as "manmade" were identified as "staircase," "building," and "glass door."
    *   Points annotated as "sidewalk" or "drivable surface" were distinguished as "road," "sidewalk," and "gate."

**Dataset-Specific Performance:**
*   **Indoor vs. Outdoor:** While we achieved state-of-the-art results on nuScenes and ScanNet200, we observed lower mIoU on the standard ScanNet (20 classes) compared to fixed-vocabulary methods. We attribute this to the difficulty of mapping a vast, auto-generated open vocabulary down to a small, coarse-grained set of 20 categories.
*   **Granularity Validation:** The performance on ScanNet200 (14.6 mIoU) was superior to baselines, confirming that the method excels when evaluated against finer-grained annotations that better match the specificity of the auto-generated vocabulary.

These points are annotated as vegetation, drivable surface, sidewalk and manmade in the original dataset (not presented here) but are misclassified as sidewalk and barrier in (b).

  - Filename: figure_2.png

Then, Caption2Tag excludes irrelevant words in the captions. The remaining nouns are passed to a text encoder and eventually assigned to points through a segmenter. The dashed lines indicate that the entire images branch is optional. The point captioner is the only trainable component in 3D-AVS. Note that, the example point caption is generated based on observing the green points.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 5:
  - Filename: figure_4.png
  - Caption: Figure 4. Sparse Masked Attention Pooling (SMAP). Given the coordinates and features of all points, a relative positional encoding (PE) is applied, followed by a residual connection. Masks are applied to the points, creating groups of point subsets. Global Average Pooling (GAP) on each subset produces a mean feature as a query. Finally, multi-head attention (MHA) is applied within each group to generate one feature per subset.
--------------------------------------------------
Item 6:
  - Filename: figure_3.png
  - Caption: Figure 3. Point Captioner Overview. The image encoder and point encoder are pre-aligned in the CLIP latent space. During training (left), Sparse Masked Attention Pooling (SMAP) aggregates features from points visible in the image (highlighted in red) and is supervised using CLIP image features. During inference (right), neither the image nor camera intrinsic parameters are available. To address this, a group of masks are generated based solely on geometric information. The SMAP output is then decoded into a group of captions. For simplicity, only one image (left) and one sector (right) are shown.
--------------------------------------------------

prompt.text:
Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

```latex
  \label{fig:short}

```

## Illustrations, graphs, and photographs
All graphics should be centered.
In \LaTeX, avoid using the \texttt{center} environment for this purpose, as this adds potentially unwanted whitespace.
Instead use
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \centering
\end{verbatim}}
```
at the beginning of your figure.

Please ensure that any point you wish to make is resolvable in a printed copy of the paper. Resize fonts in figures to match the font in the body text, and choose line widths that render effectively in print.

When placing figures in \LaTeX, it's almost always best to use \verb+\includegraphics+, and to specify the figure width as a multiple of the line width as in the example below

```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
   \usepackage{graphicx} ...
   \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]
                   {myfile.pdf}
\end{verbatim}}
```

## Color
If you use color in your plots, please keep in mind that a significant subset of reviewers and readers may have a color vision deficiency; red-green blindness is the most frequent kind.
Hence avoid relying only on color as the discriminative feature in plots (such as red \vs green lines), but add a second discriminative feature to ease disambiguation.


## Important Rules 
* DO NOT change `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleveref}` into `\usepackage[capitalize]{cleverref}`, as there's no `cleverref.sty`.
* Keep the existing packages in the template unchanged.
* For consistent compilation across environments, all figures will reside in the `figures` directory. Always include the `figures/` prefix in your `\includegraphics` command. Failing to include this prefix (e.g., using `figure_1.png` instead of `figures/figure_1.png`) will result in figure loading errors during the build process.
* Always use the following author information placeholder in your writeup:
    * Ambitious AI Researcher, AI Research Institute, 123 AI Avenue, ML City, researcher@institute.ai


Critical Constraints
1. Scientific Integrity
• All reported experimental results MUST match the provided experimental logs.
• Never fabricate results, numbers, baselines, datasets, or metrics.
• If results are weak, negative, or inconclusive, report them honestly and discuss possible explanations.
2. Literature Cutoff Rule
You must behave as if the current date is: 2024-11. Do NOT cite or discuss papers published after this date.
3. Page Limit
The main paper is limited to 8 pages (including figures and tables but excluding references and appendices). Use space efficiently while remaining concise.
4. Template Compliance
• Do not modify the overall LaTeX style or document structure mandated by the conference template.
• References must be handled through a references.bib file.
• Use standard LaTeX citation commands (e.g., \cite{}). Make sure you ONLY cite keys that exist in your generated BibTeX code block.

Section Guidelines
• Title: Concise, descriptive, and memorable. Preferably under two lines.
• Abstract: A single, compelling paragraph summarizing the problem context, proposed approach, key results, and main takeaway.
• Introduction: Introduce the problem and motivate its importance. Provide necessary background context. Clearly summarize the paper's core contributions.
• Related Work: Discuss prior work addressing similar or related problems. Detail the relationship between existing literature and the current approach. Cite relevant baselines and influential papers published before 2024-11.
• Methodology: Clearly and pedantically describe the proposed method. Provide sufficient technical depth for full reproducibility. Use equations, figures, and structured explanations when appropriate.
• Experiments: Detail the empirical setup (datasets, baselines, evaluation metrics, and implementation details). Present results faithfully based on the experimental logs. Ensure any figures located in the figures/ directory are seamlessly integrated and referenced in text.
• Conclusion: Summarize the main findings and contributions. Briefly and realistically discuss limitations and potential future directions.
• Appendix (optional): Include supplementary details that do not fit within the main page limit.

LaTeX Quality Requirements
Ensure the generated LaTeX compiles flawlessly out-of-the-box. Avoid common issues such as:

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Current perception methods for autonomous systems, particularly in the 3D domain, operate under a strict "inclusiveness assumption": they require all potential object categories to be present in the training dataset or provided as pre-defined text prompts (Open-Vocabulary Segmentation). This approach is fundamentally unscalable for dynamic real-world environments where rare, atypical, or unknown objects appear frequently. Relying on human-specified queries limits the system's autonomy, while pre-defined lists fail to capture scene-specific nuances. There is currently no framework that allows a 3D perception system to automatically generate its own vocabulary and segment a scene without human intervention or prior knowledge of the category set.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can achieve **3D Auto-Vocabulary Segmentation (3D-AVS)** by integrating Multi-Modality Large Language Models (MLLMs) directly into the segmentation pipeline. By utilizing both an image-based captioner (for rich semantic detail) and a novel geometry-based **Point Captioner** (for lighting-invariant robustness), we can dynamically generate a scene-specific vocabulary at runtime.

Furthermore, we propose that a **Sparse Masked Attention Pooling (SMAP)** module will allow the Point Captioner to effectively distill 2D vision-language knowledge into 3D features, enabling the generation of diverse, localized captions directly from sparse LiDAR data. Finally, to validate this open-ended output, we hypothesize that a CLIP-space semantic consistency metric can objectively evaluate performance without relying on rigid ground-truth label mapping.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a framework named **3D-AVS**. The pipeline processes a point cloud $\mathbf{P}$ and corresponding images $\mathbf{I}$, generates captions via dual modalities, parses them into tags, and performs segmentation.

### 1. Dual-Modality Captioning and Parsing
The system will generate a vocabulary $\mathbf{L} = \{l_m\}_{m=1}^M$ for each input scene automatically.

*   **Image Captioning:** We will utilize an off-the-shelf MLLM (specifically xGen-MM) to generate captions from the image set $\mathbf{I} \in \mathbb{R}^{K \times H \times W \times 3}$, producing captions $\mathbf{D} = \{ d_{\mathrm{im}}^{(k)} \}$.
*   **Point Captioning:** We will design a custom Point Captioner (detailed below) that takes the point cloud $\mathbf{P}$ and outputs captions $d_{\mathrm{pt}}$ based solely on geometric features, ensuring robustness in low-light conditions.
*   **Text Parsing:** The resulting natural language sentences will be processed using spaCy to extract compound and proper nouns. We will lemmatize these nouns and verify them against the WordNet dictionary to form the final tag set $\mathbf{L}$.

### 2. The Point Captioner with Sparse Masked Attention Pooling (SMAP)
The Point Captioner is the only trainable component and aims to decode text from CLIP-aligned point features. To handle the sparsity and varying scale of 3D data, we introduce the **SMAP** module.

**Feature Encoding:**
We utilize a CLIP-aligned point encoder $h_{\mathrm{pt}}$ to map points to the vision-language latent space.
$$ \mathcal{F} = \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{pt}} = h_{\mathrm{pt}}(\mathbf{P}) \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C} $$

**SMAP Architecture:**
SMAP takes point coordinates $\mathcal{C} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}$, features $\mathcal{F}$, and a set of $J$ binary masks $\mathbf{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{J \times N}$. It applies relative positional encoding (PE) and masks the features:
$$ \mathcal{F}' = \mathcal{B} * \left( \mathcal{F} + \mathrm{PE}(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{F}) \right) $$
where $*$ denotes matrix multiplication. The masked features $\mathcal{F}'$ are processed via two paths:
1.  **Key/Value:** Zero-padded to uniform length for Multi-Head Attention (MHA).
2.  **Query:** Passed through Global Average Pooling (GAP) to form a query vector.
The output is a set of pooled features $\mathbf{F}'' \in \mathbb{R}^{J \times C}$ which are decoded into captions.

**Mask Generation Strategy:**
*   **Training (2D-to-3D Distillation):** We generate masks based on camera visibility. We project points to the image plane; if a point falls within the frame, the mask value is true.
*   **Inference (Geometry-based):** Since camera intrinsics may not be available, we partition the point cloud geometrically. For outdoor scenes, we convert Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates $(\rho, \varphi, z)$ and split the scene into $T$ cylindrical sectors based on angle $\varphi$. The binary mask $b_n^t$ for point $n$ and sector $t$ is defined as:
    $$ b_{n}^{t} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \mathrm{true,} & \mathrm{if~} \frac{t}{T} 2 \pi \leq \varphi_n < \frac{t+1}{T} 2 \pi \\ \mathrm{false,} & \mathrm{otherwise.} \end{array} \right. $$

### 3. Open-Vocabulary Segmentation
Once the vocabulary $\mathbf{L}$ is generated, we perform segmentation using a retrieval-based approach. We employ three encoders: a text encoder $h_{\mathrm{tx}}$, a high-resolution image encoder $h_{\mathrm{im}}^{\mathrm{hr}}$, and the point encoder $h_{\mathrm{pt}}$.

We compute embeddings for the auto-generated vocabulary and the input data:
$$ \begin{aligned} \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{tx}} &= \{ e_m \}_{m=1}^M = h_{\mathrm{tx}}(\mathbf{L}) \\ \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{im}} &= \{ f_k \}_{k=1}^K = h_{\mathrm{im}}(\mathbf{I}) \\ \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{pt}} &= \{ f_n \}_{n=1}^N = h_{\mathrm{pt}}(\mathbf{P}) \end{aligned} $$

To leverage visual features for points, we use a point-to-pixel mapping function $\mathcal{T}: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ to lift image features to 3D, denoted as $\bar{f}_n^{\mathrm{im}}$. The final semantic label $\hat{l}_n$ for point $p_n$ is assigned by maximizing similarity across modalities:
$$ \hat{l}_{n} = \underset{m}{\mathrm{argmax}} \left( \operatorname{max} \left( \mathrm{SIM}(f_{n}, e_{m}) ~||~ \mathrm{SIM}(\bar{f}_{n}^{\mathrm{im}}, e_{m}) \right) \right) $$
where $||$ denotes concatenation and $\mathrm{SIM}$ is the dot product.

### 4. Text-Point Semantic Similarity (TPSS) Metric
To evaluate the quality of the auto-generated vocabulary without annotation bias (e.g., synonyms or hierarchies like "car" vs "vehicle"), we introduce the TPSS metric. This annotation-free metric measures the alignment between the predicted labels and the point features in the frozen CLIP space.

Given point features $\mathbf{F}$ and text embeddings $\mathbf{E}$ from the generated vocabulary, we calculate the max similarity score $S_n$ for each point:
$$ S_{n} = \underset{m}{\operatorname{max}} \left( \mathrm{SIM}(f_{n}, e_{m}) \right) $$
The final TPSS score is the mean over all points:
$$ \mathrm{TPSS}(\mathbf{P}, \mathbf{L}, g_{\mathrm{tx}}, g_{\mathrm{pt}}) = \underset{n}{\operatorname{mean}} (S_{n}) $$
where $g_{\mathrm{tx}}$ and $g_{\mathrm{pt}}$ are the frozen validation encoders.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **First Framework for 3D Auto-Vocabulary Segmentation:** We will establish a new paradigm where the perception system generates its own label space dynamically, removing the human-in-the-loop constraint.
2.  **Robust Multi-Modal Captioning:** By combining image-based VLMs with a specialized Point Captioner, the system will maintain performance in adverse conditions (e.g., night scenes) where image data is unreliable.
3.  **Geometry-Aware Feature Distillation:** The SMAP module will provide a method to distill 2D vision-language knowledge into 3D backbones while handling the variable sparsity of LiDAR data.
4.  **Novel Evaluation Methodology:** The TPSS metric will enable the objective assessment of open-ended vocabulary generation, accounting for semantic synonyms and granularity differences that standard mIoU cannot capture.

Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
network.web_access: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.

preinstalled.zh: 编排镜像：上游代码（固定提交、未改）、uv 锁定依赖、docker CLI（经 shim 给兄弟容器加代理和 CA）；agent 镜像：上游自己的 agent-cli Dockerfile
preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
